title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Business Cycles
book_title: Chapter 1: How the Business Got Here — From Joint-Sector Acid Maker to Fluorine Platform

epigraph.quote: In commodity chemistry, survival belongs to whoever controls the molecule; prosperity belongs to whoever upgrades it.
epigraph.author: Industrial Fluorine Engineering Maxim

web_blocks.html: To understand Tanfac Industries Ltd (TANFACIND), we must start on the Coromandel Coast in Cuddalore, Tamil Nadu. The company began in 1972 as a joint venture between Tamil Nadu Industrial Development Corporation (TIDCO) and the Aditya Birla Group (via Grasim Industries and Birla Group Holdings) [1][2][7]. It started plant output in the 1980s inside the SIPCOT Industrial Complex at Kudikadu, Cuddalore [2][7][15]. Tanfac had a clear import-replacement goal: supply Anhydrous Hydrofluoric Acid (AHF) and Aluminium Fluoride (AlF3) to India's growing aluminium smelters and chemical plants [2][7][15]. Consumers never see Tanfac's products, yet heavy industry cannot run without them. Primary aluminium pots, stainless steel pickling lines, oil alkylation units, and agrochemical plants all rely on fluorine molecules [2][3][26]. Very few plants hold the permits and skills to make and handle these acids safely [2][3][26].

For nearly four decades under Birla and TIDCO control, that industrial role carried a hard ceiling. Tanfac sold basic AHF and AlF<sub>3</sub> into merchant markets [1][15]. Global fluorspar swings, Chinese export surges, and local smelter cycles whipsawed its earnings [1][15][16]. The audited 12-year record from FY2015 to FY2026 makes this clear. In FY2015, Tanfac posted ₹120 crore in sales and ₹8 crore in operating profit (7% OPM) [1]. It paid ₹10 crore in interest on ₹69 crore of debt, ending with a ₹5 crore net loss and negative reserves of ₹10 crore [1]. FY2016 brought little relief. Sales edged up to ₹133 crore, operating profit stayed at ₹9 crore (7% OPM), and net profit was ₹0 crore [1]. A sharp upcycle in FY2018–FY2019 lifted sales from ₹162 crore to ₹222 crore and margins from 13% to 24% [1]. ROCE peaked at 78% as debt fell from ₹43 crore to ₹12 crore [1]. Yet FY2020 and FY2021 pulled sales right back down to ₹165 crore and ₹148 crore [1]. Throughout that legacy era, Tanfac acted as a classic price-taker. It earned strong cash in tight markets, yet could not compound capital steadily without specialty downstream products [1][2].

web_blocks.title: The 2022 Inflection: Aditya Birla Exits, Anupam Rasayan Enters
paragraphs: Everything changed in early 2022 when the Aditya Birla Group exited its non-core fluorochemicals stake [7]. Anupam Rasayan India Limited, a major Indian custom-synthesis and specialty chemical firm, bought a 24.96% controlling stake via a Share Purchase Agreement (SPA) [6][7]. It also launched a mandatory 26% SEBI open offer alongside co-promoter TIDCO [6][7].

For Anupam Rasayan, Tanfac was a key backward-integration prize rather than a passive financial bet [4][10]. Fluorine chemistry adds high value to modern farm and drug active ingredients [4][10]. Owning a coastal HF plant at Cuddalore with full green permits gave the group instant molecule security [4][10]. It avoided a five-year wait for new hazardous-chemical approvals [4][10].

web_blocks.html: The post-2022 shift happened in three clear waves that reshaped both profits and the balance sheet [1][4]. First, Tanfac wiped out its old debt. From FY2020 to FY2024, it ran debt-free and built a ₹67 crore investment cushion [1]. Second, the post-COVID fluorine upcycle met Anupam Rasayan's commercial network. Sales jumped 116% in FY2022 to ₹320 crore, then reached ₹375 crore in FY2023 and ₹378 crore in FY2024 [1]. In FY2025, sales surged 47% to ₹557 crore, with ₹131 crore in operating profit (24% OPM) and ₹88 crore in net profit [1]. Third, management pivoted from merchant acid toward captive scale and higher-value downstream fluorochemicals [4][11].

web_blocks.caption: Tanfac Industries — 12-Year Business & Margin Cycle Evolution (FY2015–FY2026) [1]
web_blocks.takeaway: Tanfac evolved from a loss-making, leveraged commodity producer in FY2015 into a ₹711 crore fluorochemical platform in FY2026, though operating margins normalized from 24% peak spreads to 16% as new capacity ramped up.

web_blocks.html: On October 7, 2024, Tanfac started a ~₹100 crore brownfield expansion funded mainly by internal cash [11]. This project doubled its core Anhydrous Hydrofluoric Acid (AHF) capacity from 14,850 MTPA to 29,700 MTPA [11]. That single step drove the FY2025–FY2026 volume surge, lifting FY2026 sales 28% to ₹711 crore [1][5]. Yet the numbers also flash a warning for careful analysts. Revenue grew from ₹557 crore in FY2025 to ₹711 crore in FY2026, and hit ₹230 crore in the September 2026 quarter [1]. Meanwhile, operating margins fell from 24% in FY2025 to 16% in FY2026 and 12% in Q2 FY2027 (Sep 2026) [1]. Peak scarcity spreads cooled just as depreciation rose from ₹10 crore to ₹17 crore [1]. Borrowings also returned to ₹93 crore in FY2026 and ₹136 crore by September 2026 to fund the next wave of downstream capex [1][4].

This next wave is the largest in Tanfac's 54-year history. In June and October 2025, Tanfac started India's first dedicated Solar-Grade Dilute Hydrofluoric Acid (DHF) plant at Cuddalore with 10,000 TPA capacity on an AHF basis [3][12]. Then, in January 2026, the board approved a ₹495 crore capex plan for a 20,000 MTPA downstream fluorinated chemicals and R-32 refrigerant gas plant [4][8][9]. A 7-year ₹2,362.5 crore supply deal with a Japanese buyer starting January 2027 anchors this expansion [4][8][9]. A ₹250 crore QIP in June 2026 and a ~₹99.41 crore preferential issue cushion the funding [4][8][9]. ICRA's October 2026 rating note highlights strong ties to Anupam Rasayan and a net debt-free post-QIP balance sheet [4]. Still, ICRA flags R-32 plant execution and ramp-up as key rating risks [4]. Tanfac now stands midway between its commodity past and a multi-client specialty future. Across the next five chapters, we will test if those new economics truly hold up.

A quarterly view from September 2023 through September 2026 sharpens this recent turn [1]. Between Q2 FY2024 (Sep 2023) and Q1 FY2025 (Jun 2024), quarterly sales stayed in a tight ₹81–₹103 crore band [1]. Operating profit held at ₹15–₹16 crore, with OPM steady at 16%–19% [1]. Once the doubled 29,700 MTPA AHF line started in October 2024, quarterly sales jumped to ₹112 crore in Q2 FY2025 at 24% OPM [1]. Sales then spiked to ₹178 crore in Q3 FY2025, delivering a cycle-peak ₹50 crore operating profit (28% OPM) and ₹35 crore net profit [1]. Quarterly revenue held at ₹172–₹193 crore through FY2026 [1]. Yet as global acid spreads cooled and Solar DHF phased in, OPM stepped down from 28% in Dec 2024 to 21% in Mar 2025 [1]. Margins averaged 15%–16% across FY2026 and dipped to 12% in Sep 2026, even as quarterly sales hit a record ₹230 crore (+37% YoY) [1].

Ownership stability evolved alongside this capacity build. Unlike private-equity turnarounds built on financial engineering, Tanfac keeps a dual-promoter structure [2][6][7]. It pairs Tamil Nadu state body TIDCO with Anupam Rasayan India Limited [2][6][7]. After the mid-2026 QIP and preferential equity issues, promoter stake shifted modestly from 51.82% (through Mar 2026) to 48.98% in Sep 2026 [1]. At the same time, institutional ownership grew fast. FII stakes rose from 0.03% to 1.40%, and DII stakes climbed from 0.33% to 3.63% [1]. Big funds now recognize Tanfac's downstream shift, even though margin cycles have not gone away [1][4].

book_paragraphs: Imagine standing at the gates of the SIPCOT Industrial Complex in Kudikadu, Cuddalore, on India's southeastern coast. The air carries salt from the Bay of Bengal. Behind the walls sits a plant that has handled hydrogen fluoride, one of the toughest molecules on the periodic table, since the 1980s. We are looking at Tanfac Industries Ltd, formed in 1972 as a joint venture between TIDCO and the Aditya Birla Group. For over forty years, Tanfac worked as an industrial back-office supplier. It fed India's aluminium smelters, steel pickling lines, and chemical plants, yet stayed out of public view.

Trace Tanfac's history through its audited accounts rather than press releases, and you see two distinct firms split by one year: 2022. Before 2022, Tanfac was a classic cyclical acid maker. It produced Anhydrous Hydrofluoric Acid and Aluminium Fluoride for price-sensitive buyers. Its margins swung hard with global fluorspar costs and Chinese imports. In FY2015, on ₹120 crore of sales, it earned just ₹8 crore in operating profit (a 7% margin). It paid ₹10 crore in interest on ₹69 crore of debt, ending with a ₹5 crore net loss and negative reserves of ₹10 crore. FY2016 was no better, with zero net profit on ₹133 crore of sales. A brief boom in FY2019 lifted sales to ₹222 crore, margins to 24%, and ROCE to 78%. Even then, the gain faded fast, and sales slipped back to ₹165 crore in FY2020 and ₹148 crore in FY2021.

Then came the 2022 ownership shift. The Aditya Birla Group exited its 24.96% stake. Anupam Rasayan India Limited, a fast-growing specialty custom-synthesis firm, stepped in as co-promoter with TIDCO and launched a 26% SEBI open offer. Why did Anupam Rasayan want an old inorganic fluoride plant in Tamil Nadu? Fluorine atoms boost stability and potency in modern farm and drug molecules. Securing green permits for a new coastal hydrofluoric acid plant from scratch takes years. Instead of waiting five years for hazardous-chemical approvals, Anupam Rasayan bought a brownfield site with four decades of active permits.

Under the new co-promoters, Tanfac's pace changed sharply. First, it repaired its balance sheet, running debt-free from FY2020 through FY2024 while building ₹67 crore in investments. Second, it rode post-pandemic fluorochemical demand. Sales more than doubled from ₹148 crore in FY2021 to ₹320 crore in FY2022. Revenue held near ₹375–₹378 crore in FY2023–FY2024, then jumped 47% to ₹557 crore in FY2025. That jump followed a ₹100 crore brownfield expansion that doubled AHF capacity from 14,850 MTPA to 29,700 MTPA in October 2024.

Here is where we must put on our skeptical lens. Between FY2025 and FY2026, revenue grew 28% to ₹711 crore, and quarterly sales reached ₹230 crore in September 2026. On the surface, that looks like smooth growth. Beneath the surface, operating profit fell from ₹131 crore in FY2025 to ₹114 crore in FY2026. Margins dropped from 24% to 16%, and slid further to 12% in the September 2026 quarter. Why? FY2025 enjoyed rare scarcity spreads, while FY2026 brought normal pricing, 70% higher depreciation from new assets, and higher input costs.

Right as base-acid margins cooled, Tanfac launched its boldest capex cycle yet. It started India's first 10,000 TPA Solar-Grade Dilute Hydrofluoric Acid plant in June and October 2025. It also signed a 7-year ₹2,362.5 crore supply deal with a Japanese buyer starting January 2027. In January 2026, the board approved ₹495 crore in capex for a 20,000 MTPA downstream fluorinated chemicals and R-32 refrigerant gas plant. A ₹250 crore QIP and a ₹99.41 crore preferential issue back that build. Our core question is whether this shift turns Tanfac into a steady specialty compounder, or traps it in a heavy capex downcycle.

Zoom in on the thirteen quarters from September 2023 through September 2026 to hear the kilns speed up at Cuddalore. For four straight quarters through June 2024, Tanfac billed ₹81 crore to ₹103 crore a quarter and earned ₹15 crore to ₹16 crore in operating profit. Then the doubled AHF line came online in October 2024. Quarterly sales leaped to ₹178 crore in December 2024, with operating profit hitting ₹50 crore and margins touching 28%. Revenue then settled into a new ₹170 crore to ₹230 crore quarterly run rate. Yet as sales hit a record ₹230 crore in September 2026, operating margins cooled to 12%. Volume scale and spread compression can clearly strike in the exact same quarter.

Meanwhile, Tanfac's shareholder base matured quietly. TIDCO and Anupam Rasayan steered the firm through its mid-2026 equity raises. Promoter ownership nudged down from 51.82% to 48.98%. At the same time, domestic and foreign funds lifted their combined stake from under 0.5% to over 5% by September 2026.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Look at the split between top-line volume and bottom-line margin in FY2026. Sales rose 28% to ₹711 crore, yet operating profit fell 13% from ₹131 crore to ₹114 crore. When revenue climbs while margins drop 800 basis points, you are watching capacity-driven volume growth collide with normal commodity spreads.

book_subsections.title: The Three Eras of Tanfac's Capital Cycle
paragraphs: We can split Tanfac's modern financial record into three clean chapters. Era One (FY2015–FY2019) was debt paydown: borrowings fell from ₹69 crore to ₹12 crore as the firm sweated legacy AHF and Aluminium Fluoride plants. Era Two (FY2020–FY2024) was a debt-free cash-build phase. It ended with the 2022 Anupam Rasayan entry and cash-funded doubling of AHF capacity.

Era Three (FY2025–FY2027E) is a high-stakes reinvestment phase. Debt returned to the balance sheet, rising from zero in FY2024 to ₹41 crore in FY2025, ₹93 crore in FY2026, and ₹136 crore by September 2026. Capital work-in-progress swelled to ₹153 crore, while reserves jumped to ₹726 crore after mid-2026 equity raises. Tanfac is no longer hoarding cash; it is betting its balance sheet on downstream fluorine chemistry.

book_subsections.title: What Past Boom-Bust Swings Teach Us About Spreads
paragraphs: Look back at FY2019 and FY2022–FY2025. Both cycles produced 24% operating margins, and both saw sharp mean reversion down to 16% in FY2020 and 16% again in FY2026. That rhythm reminds us that base hydrofluoric acid and aluminium fluoride remain spread businesses. Only differentiated downstream molecules can break that 16% ceiling for good.

book_subsections.title: Why the 2022 Ownership Shift Changed Capital Allocation
paragraphs: Before 2022, Tanfac behaved like a cautious utility focused on dividends and debt paydown. It cut debt from ₹69 crore in FY2015 to zero by FY2020, avoided big greenfield bets, and parked spare cash in safe investments. Once Anupam Rasayan joined TIDCO as co-promoter, the goal flipped from preserving cash to vertical integration.

Within three years of the 2022 open offer, Tanfac doubled AHF capacity to 29,700 MTPA and built India's first 10,000 TPA Solar-Grade DHF plant. It also committed ₹495 crore to a 20,000 MTPA downstream fluorinated chemicals facility. That speed of capital deployment would have been unthinkable before 2022. It explains both the sales surge to ₹784 crore TTM and the return of ₹136 crore in debt by September 2026.
